name: Bianca Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a team of five cable jointers in the city, so where most lineworkers are up poles, I'm mostly down holes. The power in the old harbour district runs through underground cables, and when one fails we dig it up, find the fault, cut out the bad bit and build a new joint by hand. A big joint on a twenty thousand volt cable can take me five hours, kneeling in a pit with the traffic going over my head. I like that it's careful work, like surgery with a hacksaw, and when I seal it up I know it'll still be there in forty years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of it for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pits flood, the cables are older than my grandmother, and half the maps of what's under the road are wrong. Last month we dug in the wrong spot on Quay Street for a whole morning because a drawing from 1974 was off by three metres. And being the first woman team lead at our depot means I still get the odd comment from contractors, which I've stopped caring about mostly. I go home to a shared flat, my friend Noor and her very rude cat, and I sleep like a stone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first picture is called “AI Plateau”. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we spend the money on new cables instead of software. At work there'd be a few jokes about the AI fault-finder the company trialled that kept pointing at the wrong street. Online I'd maybe post something in the union group about where the money should go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, and that's fine. I've got about four months saved and I'm putting money away for a deposit on a flat of my own. If jobs and pay carry on, I keep doing that and I'm in a good place in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, honestly. I'd keep putting four hundred a month in the deposit account and keep training my two newer jointers. Maybe I'd use the chat assistant a bit more for writing reports, because that part does save me time, but that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the fault-finder pointed at the wrong street. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was supposed to listen to the cable and tell us where the fault was. Twice it sent us to the right road but the wrong end, and the old guy on my team, Henrik, found it in ten minutes by walking along with his headphones on the old kit. We still laugh about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture you'd be sorry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If AI could fix the maps, so we stopped digging holes in the wrong place, I'd take that tomorrow. I'm not against the stuff, I just want it to work before they sell it to us.

S0.say: I'd say good, now spend the money on new cables instead of software. At work we'd joke about the AI fault-finder that kept pointing at the wrong street, and I'd post in the union group about where money should go.
S0.think: For me nothing changes, and that's fine. I've got about four months saved and I'm putting money towards a deposit, so if things carry on I'm in a good place in a few years.
S0.do: Keeps paying four hundred a month into her deposit account and keeps training her two newer jointers. Uses the chat assistant a bit more for writing reports, and otherwise carries on.
S0.quote: I'm not against the stuff, I just want it to work before they sell it to us.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca is grounded and proud of slow, careful work underground. She's open to tools that prove themselves, like better maps of buried cables, and amused by ones that don't. Her deposit savings are the quiet centre of her plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called “Steady Disruption”. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when the union earns its money. Change is fine, but the people who lose out need retraining and pay protection, and that's paid by the company, not just by them. To friends I'd say my job's fairly safe down a hole, but my cousin in the call centre isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one could make my job better. If AI sorts out the maps and the fault-finding actually works, I spend less time digging in the wrong place and more time jointing. My worry isn't really me, it's the people in planning and customer service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the tools have been tried on another team, then I'd learn them properly, the mapping and fault-finding stuff especially. I'd go to the union meetings about the changes and push for retraining money for the office staff. And I'd keep saving for the flat, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, actually. Interested, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your cousin in the call centre. What would you say to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her name's Lucie, she's twenty-four. I'd tell her to get onto any course the company offers before the cuts come, not after, because the good places go first. And I'd tell her to join the union, which she keeps saying she'll do and doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until another team tries the tools first. Why not be first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been first at things before and it's tiring. I was the first woman lead, I don't need to be the first person to debug a buggy app as well. Let the city north depot find the problems, and I'll learn it once it works.

S1.say: I'd say this is when the union earns its money: people who lose out need retraining and pay protection paid by the company. To friends I'd say my job's fairly safe down a hole, but my cousin in the call centre isn't.
S1.think: I think this one could make my job better, if AI fixes the maps and fault-finding. My worry isn't really me, it's the people in planning and customer service.
S1.do: Waits for another depot to trial the new mapping and fault-finding tools, then learns them properly. Goes to union meetings to push for retraining money for office staff, and keeps saving for the flat.
S1.quote: I was the first woman lead, I don't need to be the first person to debug a buggy app as well.
S1.fieldNote: Her steady streak is deliberate, not fearful: she's tired of being first. Her political instincts point outward to office staff and her cousin. She sees steady change as possibly improving her own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called “AGI by 2028”. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency action, like in a pandemic. Wage support, a pause on layoffs at public utilities, and a say for workers in how the robots are brought in. I'd say that at work, at the union, and I'd be marching if there was a march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd admit at the depot. I always told myself nobody can automate kneeling in a flooded pit, but if a robot can do almost anything a person can, then the pit is just another job. And all my plans, the flat, maybe a family one day, they sit on a wage I might not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the flat search straight away and keep the deposit money as an emergency fund, so that four months becomes more like eight. I'd push hard in the union for a deal on job guarantees. I'd look for the jobs nearest to mine that the robots still need someone for, like testing, commissioning or safety checks, and get on any course for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor's gone soft under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean to give up on the flat for now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd hurt. I've been looking for two years, I've got a spreadsheet with every viewing. But I'd rather be renting with Noor and have savings than own a flat I can't pay for if the job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at your depot would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Henrik. He's sixty-one, he's got four years to his pension and he's never touched a computer he didn't have to. Two years would wipe him out right before the finish line, and nobody's going to retrain a man two years from retirement.

S2.say: I'd say we need emergency action like in a pandemic: wage support, a pause on layoffs at public utilities, and a worker say in how robots come in. I'd say it at the union and march if there was a march.
S2.think: It scares me more than I'd admit at the depot. If a robot can do almost anything, then the flooded pit is just another job, and my plans for a flat and maybe a family sit on a wage I might not have.
S2.do: Stops the flat search and keeps the deposit as an emergency fund, stretching four months of cover towards eight. Pushes in the union for job guarantees and gets on a course for testing, commissioning or safety work.
S2.feel: Alarmed, as if the floor has gone soft under her.
S2.quote: I always told myself nobody can automate kneeling in a flooded pit, but if a robot can do almost anything a person can, then the pit is just another job.
S2.fieldNote: A clear gap between say and think: publicly she's organising, privately she's frightened. Giving up the flat search, with its spreadsheet of viewings, is a real loss she names plainly. Her worry for Henrik shows how she measures harm by who is closest to the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called “AGI by 2031”. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for chaos. Governments and companies should be planning now, retraining people properly and sharing out the gains. I'd keep saying it in the union and to anyone who'll listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is about the time I'd need to get a second skill. I'd be thirty-two, that's young. It's still a gamble, because nobody knows which jobs stay human, but at least it's a gamble I'd have time to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep working, keep saving, and watch which jobs the robot companies are struggling with. I'd probably put the flat on hold for a year to see how fast things move. By year two I'd pick a course, I'm leaning towards network control or commissioning, and I'd ask the union to get the company to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. Like the night before a big job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put the flat on hold for a year. What would make you start looking again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If by the end of that year the robots still can't do the messy real-world stuff, digging in old streets, wrong maps, water everywhere, I'd feel safer. Then I'd buy, maybe something smaller. If they can, I'd keep renting and keep the money liquid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why network control or commissioning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone still has to decide when power goes on and off, and answer for it if it goes wrong. I've stood in enough pits waiting for the control room to give me the okay to know it matters. And I'd still be in the industry I know.

S3.say: I'd say five years means there's no excuse for chaos: governments and companies should plan now, retrain people properly and share the gains. I'd keep saying it in the union and to anyone who'll listen.
S3.think: Five years is about the time I'd need to get a second skill, and thirty-two is young. It's still a gamble, because nobody knows which jobs stay human, but I'd have time to think about it.
S3.do: Keeps working and saving in year one, puts the flat on hold to see how fast things move, and watches what robots struggle with. By year two picks a course in network control or commissioning and asks the union to get the company to pay.
S3.feel: Anxious but workable, like the night before a big job.
S3.quote: Someone still has to decide when power goes on and off, and answer for it if it goes wrong.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn fear into a plan she can work through. She uses the first year as a test, tied to whether robots can handle the messiness of old streets. Network control appeals because it's about responsibility, not just skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called “AGI by 2036”. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, so let's do it fairly. A shorter working week, retraining for everyone who wants it, and a share of the savings for the people whose jobs go. I'd say it at the depot and I'd probably get more involved in the union nationally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years doesn't scare me much. I'd be thirty-seven, I could have a whole second career by then, or move into something next to this one. I'd still be sad about the jointing, though, because it's the thing I'm best at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat, actually, because ten years of wages is a long time and I'd have a fixed mortgage. Around year three or four I'd start a part-time course in network control. And I'd learn whatever AI tools come in on the job, once they're proven, so I'm the one who knows how they work when the change comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. More sad than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years doesn't scare you, but you're also starting a course in year three. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. It doesn't scare me because I'd have time to do something about it, and the course is the something. If I did nothing, then yes, I'd be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most about jointing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quiet bit at the end, when you've built a joint layer by layer and you put your hand on it before you backfill the hole. Nobody will ever see it again. I like knowing it's mine and it's holding up a whole street.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly: a shorter working week, retraining for everyone who wants it, and a share of the savings for people whose jobs go. I'd get more involved in the union nationally.
S4.think: Ten years doesn't scare me much, because at thirty-seven I could have a whole second career. I'd still be sad about jointing, because it's the thing I'm best at.
S4.do: Buys the flat on a fixed mortgage, trusting ten years of wages. Starts a part-time network control course around year three or four, and learns new AI tools once they're proven so she understands them early.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, more sad than scared.
S4.quote: Nobody will ever see it again. I like knowing it's mine and it's holding up a whole street.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she flips to buying the flat, a strong sign that time, not the end point, drives her fear. She answers the contradiction neatly: the plan is what removes the fear. The pride in her joints carries real grief.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Not because it's the end, they're all the same end, but because two years gives nobody time, not me, not Henrik, not the government. What would help is wage support while you retrain, and a law that public utilities can't just dump their workers the minute the robots work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the maps. Seriously. If AI fixed the maps of what's under our streets, it would save more money than any robot jointer, and we'd stop digging up the wrong road. Nobody ever asks the people in the hole what would actually help.

headlineQuote: A big joint on a twenty thousand volt cable can take me five hours, kneeling in a pit with the traffic going over my head.
portrait: Bianca Dubois is a 27-year-old team lead of five cable jointers on the city's underground network, and the first woman lead at her depot. She shares a flat with her friend Noor and has about four months saved towards a deposit. She's open to new tools once they've been proven elsewhere and thinks of union action first when others are hurt. She's calm through the milder pictures, alarmed by AGI in two years because her flat and future plans rest on her wage, and steadily less worried as the warning time grows, to the point of buying the flat with ten years' notice.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years gives nobody time to prepare, not her, not older colleagues like Henrik, and not the government.
whatWouldHelp: Wage support while people retrain, and a law stopping public utilities from dumping workers as soon as robots work.
